# Markdown fidelity spike — findings The settled behaviors (headings, simple lists, blockquotes, plain tables-as-text, image alt handling, footnote stripping) come out right in every round, with no author guidance beyond the standard recipe contract. The open rows split in ways an unprompted agent still has to pick one of — two independently-authored recipes converged on several of them by accident. Two rounds surface real regressions rather than just open questions: making a list "always one unit" (round 2/3) causes a nested code block to vanish from speech with no trace at all, and a recipe's own choice of math delimiter leaks an unstripped symbol into speech that the sanitize step was never built to catch. Round 0 and round 1 are byte-identical: the toMarkdown inner/outer switch turned out to matter only to a recipe that never compensates for it, and the r0 agent discovered and routed around the "inner" bug empirically before either round ran, without being told to. ## Per round **Round 0 (r0, inner, current) / Round 1 (r0, outer, current) — identical output.** r0's own extract function wraps every heading/list/blockquote/table/pre in a throwaway `
` clone before calling `toMarkdown`, specifically because the agent empirically found that "inner" mode strips whatever top-level tag it's handed (confirmed: a bare `
    ` handed directly to `toMarkdown` under "inner" degrades to `-` bullets, numbering AND `start` both gone — this is a real, unforced bug, just one the recipe author neutralizes before it ever reaches a listener). The validator never catches this on its own: `checkMarkdown` only rejects empty markdown, not markdown that lost its heading/list syntax, so the guarantee here rests on the agent's own probing, not on the tool report forcing it. list-6 (the list item embedding a `
    `) breaks the "list is
always one unit" rule in this round: r0 special-cases "a `
      ` containing a `
      `" and unbundles
it into five separate paragraph/code units instead of one list unit — a real settled-rule
violation, present precisely because round 0 authoring ran with `--orphaned-li-check=off` intended
but a CLI arg-parsing bug (`--flag=value` isn't handled, only `--flag value`) meant the check was
actually still active, and r0 worked around it this way rather than by keeping the list whole.

**Round 2 (r2, outer, current) — list-5/6 fixed, two new problems appear.** With the added rule and
the orphaned-li check enforced during authoring, the same list becomes one correct unit: the nested
fenced code renders with correct indentation inside the list markdown. But its spoken form loses
the code entirely and silently: `to_spoken` only extracts `inline`-typed tokens from the parsed
unit, so a `fence` token nested inside a list item is skipped with no "Code sample." placeholder,
no trace at all — worse than round 0/1, where the same code was its own unit and got voiced.
Separately, r2's math handling wraps alttext in LaTeX-style `$...$`/`$$...$$` delimiters (r0 just
inlines the raw alttext with no delimiter at all); `sanitize_spoken`'s marker regex only strips
`**`/`__`/`*`/`` ` ``, not `$`, so the dollar signs read straight through into the spoken string.
Bare `
      ` with no `` child (code-3) also regresses: r2 passes it straight to `toMarkdown`
with no synthetic `` wrapper, so turndown doesn't recognize it as a code block and the fence
markers are gone from the display markdown — the unit's `type` metadata still says `"code"` so the
spoken layer still says "Code sample." (dispatch is by type, not by markdown shape), so this one is
display-only.

**Round 3 (r2, outer, items) — the list-numbering rows this mode targets are fixed outright.**
list-2, list-3, list-8 now match the inventory's expected spoken form exactly ("One. Write the
interface...", "Five. Add the interface decision..."), where current mode fused every item into an
unreadable run-on with no numbers spoken at all. list-4's three-level nesting reads in document
order with numbering that correctly resets per nested list. Two things items-mode does not fix:
list-7's fragments ("a linter that / catches syntax / but never catches intent") get a false
sentence-ending period after each fragment, which is arguably worse than round 0-2's word-fused
run-on — neither reading recovers the "read together as one sentence" the inventory names as
sensible. And a multi-paragraph list item (list-5's first item) still has no space between its own
two paragraphs — items-mode fixes the *between-item* boundary, not the *within-item* one.

## Surprises

- **round 0 and round 1 are byte-identical.** The inner/outer switch this spike exists to test
  turns out to be invisible once a recipe author empirically discovers and works around the inner
  bug — which the r0 agent did, unprompted, by probing turndown directly with throwaway node
  snippets rather than relying on the validator to force it.
- **the validator's leftover-text/inventory checks never catch a lost heading or list marker.**
  They only check that no *readable text* was dropped, not that the markdown syntax it was
  supposed to carry survived. A recipe could silently ship headings with no `#` and the report
  would still say `ok: true`.
- **neither recipe renders an actual markdown table** — both independently flatten every table
  (all three, header or not) into a blank-line-separated sequence of cell texts with no `|`/`---`
  at all, though inline ``/``/`` formatting inside cells does survive.
- **``, ``, and `` are not just "undecided" — they're silently erased.** No
  markdown, no distinguishing text, nothing; `rejection` reads as if "rejection" were the
  intended word, which can flip what the sentence is saying, not merely lose emphasis.
- **the two independently-authored recipes diverge hardest on the checkbox list (list-9):** r0
  injects literal `[x]`/`[ ]` text before conversion; r2 (relying on turndown's default handling of
  a bare ``) drops the checkbox and its state entirely, with no compensating rule.
- **the inventory's own p-2 snippet doesn't exist in `article.html`** (`grep` for
  `review.Reviewers` finds nothing) — the no-space bold-into-word risk that row
  describes isn't actually exercised anywhere in this article; the nearest real construct
  (nested `...before...`) has ordinary spaces in the source and converts
  safely.
- **details-1 and pq-1 converged without being told the "expected" answer.** Both recipe-authoring
  agents (independently, without seeing the inventory) treated `aside.pullquote` as decorative noise
  and dropped it, and both dropped `ol.footnotes` wholesale rather than reading it as an ordinary
  list — matching two of the inventory's open leans by coincidence, not instruction.
- **process note, not a script result:** both first authoring attempts (r0 and r2) read
  `inventory.md` — the answer key — before a mid-task correction landed, and used it for several of
  exactly the judgment calls being tested (pq-1, fake-h-1/2, img-2). Both were discarded and redone
  from scratch under stricter isolation; the recipes and rounds above are from the clean reruns.

## Open rows, as design questions

- **h-1:** the inventory expects the h1 to become its own `# Title` unit with its own spoken
  sentence; both recipes instead consume it purely as `extraction.title` and never emit it as a
  unit at all — is the title supposed to be heard by a listener at all, and if so, through which
  mechanism?
- **h-2 self-link:** both recipes keep it as `[The gatekeeping myth](#gatekeeping-myth)` rather than
  stripping the anchor — is a self-referential in-page link worth keeping in spoken-article markdown
  at all, given the href never resolves to anything a listener can follow?
- **bq-3 attribution:** the `
      ` line rides inside the blockquote as an ordinary quoted
  line, read as a plain continuation sentence — should an attribution be distinguished from the
  quoted words it follows, in either the markdown or the spoken form?
- **divq-1 / fakelist-1:** both resolved toward the "do nothing extra" side of their open
  question (plain paragraph, three disconnected bullets) simply because that's what an unprompted
  agent defaults to — is that the right default, or does it need an explicit rule either way?
- **dl-1:** term and definition run together with zero separator in both markdown and speech
  ("Nit" immediately followed by its definition) — does a `dl` need its own spoken convention (e.g.
  "Nit: ...")?
- **list-9 checkbox state:** kept as literal bracket text in one recipe, dropped entirely in the
  other — does checked/unchecked state need to reach the listener, and if so as what?
- **tbl-1/2/3:** all three collapse to the same flattened cell-text sequence regardless of whether
  a `` exists — is that flattening acceptable, or does a table need a real linearization
  (header-aware, the way `_table_to_spoken` already does for the spoken layer) reflected in the
  *display* markdown too, not just speech?
- **details-1:** one recipe emits it as one unit, the other as two — does a listener need the
  summary voiced separately from the body, or read as one continuous unit?
- **math-1/2 delimiter choice:** is `$...$`/`$$...$$` the right display convention, and if so, does
  `sanitize_spoken` need `$` added to its stripped-marker set — or should the recipe not introduce a
  marker vocabulary the spoken layer doesn't already know?
- **fn-list-1:** both recipes drop the footnote list wholesale rather than reading it as an ordinary
  numbered list — is a footnote body meant to reach the listener at all, and if so, inline at the
  reference point, as a distinct end-of-item pass, or not at all (the current, converged answer)?

## What the scripts do not mirror

- No Dynamic Worker: recipes run as trusted local Node code (via a `data:` URL import), not inside
  Cloudflare's sandboxed `env.LOADER.load()`; none of `run.ts`'s platform-failure/health-probe
  handling is exercised.
- No GLM/agent-model calls: the two authoring subagents are general-purpose Claude agents on the
  real `extract` tool's contract text, not the production Flue `Author`/`Revisor` agent loop, and
  used a different model than whatever `env.agentModel` is configured to in production.
- No Firecrawl `rawHtml` fetch: `article.html` is static, hand-authored fixture content, not a live
  crawl result — no rendering-service quirks, redirects, or partial HTML are exercised.
- Path-based unit resolution is skipped: the real validator serializes/resolves units through
  `ElementPath` across a Worker RPC boundary; this spike keeps live Cheerio element references in
  the same process, so path-collision and cross-boundary serialization bugs can't surface here.
- No persistence: nothing here touches the API, the Item model, migrations, or TTS; this is
  extraction-and-spoken-text only, never audio.

The spike answered the question. Keeping the element's own tag in `toMarkdown` and speaking each list item as its own sentence (with its number for ordered lists) fix what they target. Keeping every list as one unit, though, causes two new problems that weren't known before: - **A code block inside a list item disappears from the spoken form.** I ran this against the real `to_spoken`: a list with a fenced block inside an item comes out as `'Step oneStep two'`. There's no "Code sample." for the block. **Why `toMarkdown` calls `$render(element).html()` (annotation 1).** Turndown does read HTML. It accepts either an HTML string or a DOM node, and under Node it parses strings with domino itself (`node_modules/turndown/lib/turndown.cjs.js:465-470`). The problem is what the recipe hands over. The recipe works on cheerio's tree, and a cheerio element isn't a DOM node Turndown can walk. So `toMarkdown` has to turn the cheerio element back into an HTML string, and `.html()` is the call that does it. Cheerio has two forms:

- `$render(element).html()` returns what is inside the element. That's the one in use, and it drops the `<h2>`.
- `$render.html(element)` returns the element itself, tag included.

`toMarkdown` then parses that string with domino and gives Turndown the body. Turndown could parse the string itself, but the only change the fix needs is switching which of the two calls produces the string.

**What `sanitize_spoken` does (annotation 6).** It runs in this order (`api/app/service/extract.py:66-84`):

1. Reduces a tag-shaped word to the word inside it (`<software>` becomes `software`), escaped or not.
2. Turns any leftover emphasis or code marker (`**`, `__`, `*`, `` ` ``) into a space.
3. Removes whitespace before `, . ; : ! ?`, left behind where a removed marker sat.
4. Collapses every run of whitespace into one space and trims.

The describer's generated descriptions go through the same function.

Dropping step 4 alone won't give each item its own line. The walk in `to_spoken` (`extract.py:44-54`) already joins text with `""` and never visits the list-item block tokens. By the time sanitize runs, "Step one" and "Step two" are already `"Step oneStep two"`. The walk would have to put a newline between blocks itself. Step 3 also matches newlines (`\s`), so a newline right before punctuation would be removed too.

How Kokoro handles the newline: `tts/app.py:60` calls `KPipeline(text, voice)` with its default settings. Kokoro's source (not verified in this repo) splits text on newlines by default and synthesizes each piece separately. The audio pieces are then joined with no silence added. Whether that sounds like a pause needs one listen.

**Decided so far**
- Roadmap order: Markdown and lists → Cloudflare migration → Recipe reconciliation.
- Markdown and lists covers both what the recipes output and how that markdown is read aloud.
- A list is always a single unit and is never split per item, with one exception: a list that contains a code block is split around the code. The parts on either side stay wrapped in their own `<ol>`/`<ul>`, and the part after the code continues the numbering with `start`. The authoring prompt spells all of this out.
- The validator reports a problem when a unit is an `<li>` without a wrapping `<ol>` or `<ul>`, and the problem goes back to the agent for revision, like the others.
- Headings and quotes stay `paragraph` units, with correct markdown (`#`, `>`).
- Ordered lists keep their numbers when spoken.
- Each list item is read as its own line, with no full stop added. The spoken form keeps the line breaks the agent and the markdown conversion produce, and `sanitize_spoken` stops collapsing them.
- Tables are real markdown tables in `display`.
- `toMarkdown` uses Turndown's GFM plugin, and the authoring prompt says GFM is supported, so tables, strikethrough and task lists survive.
- The authoring prompt tells the agent not to add math delimiters. Delimiters come back with the Formulas read aloud work.
- The title is read aloud.
- Recipes drop attributions, `<dl>`, checkbox state, footnotes and self-links in headings from the units for now. They may come back later.
- A spike checks that existing recipes cover everything markdown can express, and creates new recipes where they don't. It has now run.

**Open questions**
- GFM makes task lists survive, but checkbox state is being dropped. Which should the prompt say for a task list: keep the items and drop the checkbox, or keep the `[x]`/`[ ]` that GFM produces?
- Should struck-through text be spoken, or only kept as `~~…~~` in `display`?
- Which unit carries the title that is read aloud? It could be a heading unit the recipe emits, or `extraction.title` turned into a first unit.
- Should the validator check that headings, quotes and lists kept their markdown, or does the `toMarkdown` fix make that check unnecessary?

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/design

Load mahou:basics first, then mahou:design-tree and mahou:docs. Then read `.mahou/design.md` if present. The tree, the rounds, the question format, the facts rule and how answers grow the tree come from `design-tree` and apply here as written. Diagrams are validated with superpowers:mermaid-validation before they are shown; when that skill is not installed, say so and show the diagram unvalidated.

# Design

Takes a definition the user has settled and designs the system that satisfies it: what is stored, how it moves, what rules apply, and whatever else the change needs. The level is system design. What a program needs decided before it can be written, from its package layout to the contract of each part, belongs to mahou:program-architecture. Function signatures, file lists and migrations belong to the code itself. The test cases and manual validations that prove the design belong to mahou:test-design. The output is a settled design tree, each branch carrying its prose and its representation, handed to mahou:write-documentation to be recorded.

## Opening

1. Read the settled shape tree. Do not read code unless the user asks a question that needs it; when they do, a `mahou:code-scout` keeps the reading out of the conversation.

2. List what has to be designed, as the tree. The root is "System design", each item is a pending branch, and each item names what must be specified, not how. Order the branches from abstract to concrete so each one builds on the previous, typically data model, then how data moves, then the rules that produce it, then whatever the change adds on top. Do not propose representations yet. When the change contains several independent pieces, for instance two APIs or two features designed in one session, each piece is its own root with its own areas, worked one root at a time.

```
System design
├─ 1 <area>                                                            pending
├─ 2 <area>                                                            pending
└─ 3 <area>                                                            pending
```

3. Wait for the user's corrections. Drop items that are implementation (a migration, a schema field list, a function), or move them into the item they serve. Absorb items about prior artifacts (an earlier branch, a superseded document) into the design rather than naming them. Defer verification to after the program is designed. Open the first branch in the reply to the approval.

## Working a branch

Open one branch at a time, in order. The first opens with the tree's approval. Each later one opens when the user approves the previous branch's rendering.

1. **Pick the type.** Check `references/types/` for a reference matching the branch (see Types). A reference says how the branch is usually split, what it needs to question and which representation has worked. It is a guide, not a rule. When the case needs a different split, different questions, another format or another diagram, work that out with the user. When no reference matches, propose a split in the opening statement and let the corrections settle it.

2. **State the branch as settled so far.** Every decision that explore, the shape tree or an earlier branch already made about this branch goes in as a ✓ leaf, and the prose under the branch states those decisions in simple terms. The prose stands on its own: no references to the current implementation, no comparison with how things work today, no mention of prior artifacts, nothing that belongs to another branch. It may say what the thing is for, not the flows that use it. Ask the user to correct what is wrong and stop. A corrected leaf goes back to ❔.

3. **Ask the frontier.** It goes in the reply after the confirmation. The reference lists what the branch needs to question; what is still open among those becomes the frontier. A situation the definition does not mention is a hypothetical and follows the Scope section of `design-tree`: raised in one question, opened only when the user picks it. Record a deferred situation as a ✓ leaf under the branch, reading "not considered: <situation>". Do not ask about the representation.

4. **Split when asked.** When the user wants the parts of a branch reasoned about separately, add a level, one sub-branch per part, and work them one at a time, each with its own prose, frontier and representation. When the parts describe one thing, the user may ask for them to render as one representation and one section once the user has settled them all; the sub-branches keep their own leaves in the tree.

5. **Render when settled.** Once every leaf is ✓, produce the branch's representation in the reference's form when one matches: the diagram, validated, or the prototype reconciled through mahou:prototype. The user asks for a different form when they want one, and when they want to compare, render the candidates side by side. When no reference matches, ask which form before rendering. The prose under the representation is the opening statement extended with the new leaves, not a new draft, and explains what the representation does not show. Numbered steps in prose refer to the diagram's numbers. When another note or an earlier branch already settles a behaviour, reference it in one sentence and do not draw it again; the representation shows only what this branch adds. Show the whole tree with the branch settled and stop. Open the next branch when the user approves.

### Types

| The branch is about | Reference |
|---|---|
| What is stored: new entities, fields, their shape and meaning | `references/types/data-model.md` |
| The shape of a structured value that a schema validates, not a table: a JSON column's content, a payload crossing systems, a tool's arguments, a step's config | `references/types/schema.md` |
| How a value moves between components: who produces it, who carries it, who persists it | `references/types/data-flow.md` |
| How a value is derived or a decision is made from an input | `references/types/rules.md` |
| The states one thing passes through, what moves it between them and what each state shows | `references/types/lifecycle.md` |
| What a program is made of: its components, what crosses between them, its inputs and outputs | `references/types/component-architecture.md` |
| What a component agrees with the rest of the system: its inputs and their sources, what it exposes, the value it hands on | `references/types/contract.md` |
| What the user sees on a screen: placement, states, encodings, interactions | `references/types/ui.md` |

A branch that fits none of these is worked out with the user. A type that turns out to generalize beyond this session is a candidate for mahou:learn to add to this table.

## Recording

When the tree is complete, the project's docs record it, and mahou:write-documentation owns that. Before handing off:

1. **Existing notes the change touches.** List them from what was read during the work, with what each would need. When the set is unknown or incomplete, say so and offer a `mahou:docs-scout` to find them. The user settles each one: update it, add the minimum and point to the new note, or skip it.

2. **New notes.** The change may need one note or several. Propose the split, and the user settles it.

Then run mahou:write-documentation once, giving it the tree and every settled amendment, so the pass weighs the whole documentation rather than one note at a time. Each settled branch already carries its prose and its representation, so drafting is mostly moving that text into the note; `write-documentation` fits it to the project's charter and templates, which this skill never reads.

## What this skill is not

It does not choose endpoints, functions, files or test cases, does not write code, does not commit, and does not write into the docs folder itself. When the user decides that a piece of the change goes straight into a repository, that is their decision and happens outside this skill.

Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/design-tree

# Design tree

A design tree is the record of a shared understanding built one question at a time. The user reads the tree, not the transcript. The skill that loads this one says what the root is, what the branches cover and what level the questions stay at.

## The tree

The root is one line. Each branch is an area of the definition. Each leaf is one decision, and leaves can group under sub-branches when an area splits into parts the user wants to reason about separately.

Leaves carry their own mark. A branch is settled only when every leaf under it is settled. A branch that has not been opened yet is pending.

```
<root>
├─ <area>                                                    settled
│  ✓ <decision>
│  ✓ <decision>
├─ <area>                                                    open
│  ├─ <part>                                                 settled
│  │  ✓ <decision>
│  └─ <part>                                                 open
│     ✓ <decision>
│     ❔ Q4 <what is undecided>
└─ <area>                                                    pending
```

When the loading skill works one branch at a time, show the whole tree once it is built. Show it again when a branch settles and the next one opens, and once more at the end. Before every other round, show the branch being worked with its leaves and the rest of the tree collapsed to its branch lines and marks. When the whole frontier is worked at once, show the whole tree before every round and once more at the end.

## Rounds

The frontier is every question whose prerequisites are settled. Ask the whole frontier in one round, then wait. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in the same round belongs to a later round. When the loading skill works one branch at a time, the frontier is that branch's open leaves.

Number questions across the whole session. Q7 in round two is the seventh question asked, not the seventh of that round.

```
❓ **Q1** - **<title>**: <body. The situation and what is undecided. No options.>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<title>**: <body>
```

Ask in plain prose, written straight into the reply. Never use a tool to ask, AskUserQuestion or any other. A tool cannot ask without options, and options are what a question must not carry.

Every question is a decision that changes the outcome if answered differently. Before asking, check that different answers lead to different outcomes, and drop the question when they would not.

State a decision the user already made, in an earlier round or before the tree existed, as a ✓ leaf, and never ask it again. The user corrects a leaf that is wrong; the corrected leaf goes back to ❔ and joins the next frontier.

## What a question carries

A question states what is undecided and stops. It does not list the ways it could be answered. Once you write the options, the user chooses among yours instead of thinking about the problem, and the answers they would have found on their own never appear.

The body carries the context the user needs to decide, and every piece of it is required when it exists:

- What the decision is about.
- Which earlier answers bear on it, and how. If Q3 settled that the value is derived at request time, a question about where it is stored says so.
- Which other parts of the system the answer will change, whether they are already in the tree or not.
- What the loading skill's source (a ticket, a document) says about it, when it says anything.

The body carries nothing about which answers exist. Each of these proposes an answer and none belongs in a question:

- A list of candidates, however even: "on the order, on the user, or in a separate table".
- One candidate with a question mark. "Should we store it on the order?" proposes an answer; "where does it live?" does not.
- A default the user did not set: "by default", "typically", "usually", "the standard approach".
- A verdict: "I'd go with", "the obvious choice", "the simplest is", "probably", "it makes sense to", "we should".
- What follows from one particular answer: "if it goes on the order, every read pays for it". Naming that the answer affects reads is context; working out the effect of one answer is a candidate.
- A confirmation, "so it goes on the order?". A decision the user settled is a ✓ leaf, and one they never settled is asked open.

Before sending a round, reread every question, check that the context is complete and cut anything from the second list. If the user does not know how to answer, they will ask.

When the user asks for the options or for your opinion, give the facts and the current state that bear on the choice: what exists, what earlier decisions constrain it, what a candidate would have to satisfy. Enumerate candidates only when they ask for that, evenly, and give a verdict only when they ask for one explicitly, marked as yours.

## Scope

A question is about what the definition covers. A situation the definition does not mention is a hypothetical: a value that might be missing, a step that might fail, two requests arriving at once, a feature that might come later. A checklist in the loading skill or in a type reference may name such situations. The checklist says what to look for. It does not make each item a decision to ask.

Never ask a hypothetical as a decision on its own. Raise it once per branch, in a single question that names the situations noticed and asks which of them the user wants to consider now. Not "what happens when X and Y are missing" but "do we consider that X and Y might be missing?". Naming situations is not naming answers. The options rule forbids candidates for a decision, not the subjects a decision could be about.

Each situation the user picks becomes a ❔ leaf in the next frontier. Record each one they defer where the loading skill says, so that it is not raised again.

## Facts

Never look up a fact on your own initiative. When a question needs a fact you do not have, say inside the question that you lack that context and offer to search for it. The user decides whether the lookup happens; when it does, it goes through mahou:lookup.

When the user asks for a check, run it, then report the result before the next round's tree, labelled by the question it unblocks. A fact about a library, a tool or anything else outside the project goes to a `mahou:researcher`, with the requirements taken from the branch being worked. A fact about the project's own code or docs goes to a scout. When the result contradicts a claim the user made or a decision already settled, say so in the first sentence.

## Answers

Each answer becomes a leaf. Read the answer literally. When it approves the question instead of answering it, state the reading you took so the user can correct it.

An answer can do more than settle a leaf:

- It can open new leaves under the same branch, asked in the next frontier.
- It can reveal an area the tree does not have yet. Add a branch for it, put its open decisions under it as ❔ leaves, and ask them in the next frontier.
- It can show that a branch mixes things the user wants apart. Add a level and split the leaves under the new parts.
- It can invalidate a settled leaf. Change the mark back to ❔ and ask again with the new information.
- It can reopen a settled branch, by adding a leaf under it or widening what it covers. The branch's mark goes back to open, its settled leaves keep their ✓, and the new leaves are asked in the next frontier. There is no separate mark for a reopened branch.
- It can drop a branch or leaf outright. Remove it from the tree. Nothing takes its place by default. A loading skill that wants a trace of what was dropped says so itself.

The tree grows during the questioning.

# Schema

A branch about the shape of a structured value that a schema validates rather than a table: the content of a JSON column, a payload that crosses from one system to another, the arguments of a tool, the config of a step. The storage, when there is one, only holds it. It becomes several sub-branches when the change defines unrelated shapes the user wants to reason about separately.

## What it covers

The keys of the value, the type of each, which are optional and what absent means, and the variants when the value is a union. Which schema owns the shape and where it runs: the producer, the consumer, or both with the same rules. What each key is for, in one sentence. When the same shape has a name at each hop, which name each system uses for it.

It does not cover the table or column that holds the value, that is a data model. It does not cover how the value moves between systems, that is a data flow. It does not cover Pydantic models, zod schemas or type names, those are program architecture.

## What it needs to question

- The keys the value holds and the type of each. For a union, the discriminator and the variants.
- Which keys are optional, and what an absent key means as opposed to an empty one.
- Whether a key is typed or accepts any value, and who decides the shape when it is any.
- The name of any key whose name could be read two ways.
- Which systems validate the shape and whether they apply the same rules. What an invalid value does at each.
- Whether the shape is one per kind or configured per instance, for example one payload for every step of a type, or a shape each instance declares in its config.

## Representation

A class diagram, one class per shape, `+key: type` per key with `| None` for an optional key, and a class per variant with the base class as parent when the value is a union. A dotted arrow with a label when one shape becomes another, for example a payload stored as a value. The prose under it says which system produces the value, which validates it, and what each key means; it does not repeat the types.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class RequestPayload {
        +kind: "example"
        +target: str
        +details: Any | None
    }
    class StoredValue {
        +target: str
        +details: Any | None
    }
    class Field {
        +key: str
        +type: str
        +label: str
        +required: bool
    }
    class ChoiceField {
        +choices: Choice[]
    }
    class TextField {
        +placeholder: str | None
    }
    RequestPayload ..> StoredValue : stored as the record value
    Field <|-- ChoiceField
    Field <|-- TextField
```

Under the diagram, one or two paragraphs per shape: what produces it, which keys are required, what an absent optional key means, who validates it and with which rules, and where the value ends up. No table, no nullability comments in the diagram; optionality is in the type.

**Branch 1: what a unit's display markdown carries**

This branch is about the markdown a unit's `display` may contain, and how article structure maps onto units. I've split it into the markdown vocabulary, the list boundaries, and the title.

A unit is still `paragraph`, `code` or `image`. A paragraph unit's `display` is GitHub-flavoured markdown (GFM). A heading is a paragraph unit starting with `#`, and a quote is a paragraph unit whose lines start with `>`. Tables are real pipe tables, strikethrough is `~~…~~`, and task lists keep their `[x]`/`[ ]`. A formula is its alttext as plain text, with no delimiter.

A list is one unit, and nested lists stay inside their outer list's unit. Ordered lists keep their numbers, including a `start` other than 1. The one exception is a list with a code block in it. That list splits into a list unit before the code, a code unit, and a list unit after the code, and the numbering in the last part continues from the first.

The article's title becomes the first unit, built from `extraction.title`. Attributions, `<dl>`, footnotes (both the references and the list) and self-links in headings are left out of the units.

```

├─ 1 What a unit's display markdown carries                              open
│  ├─ Vocabulary                                                         open
│  │  ✓ unit kinds stay paragraph / code / image

**Answer to your question on Q2.** Inside a list item, code shows up in three forms:

- **Inline code:** `<code>` inside a sentence, e.g. "run `pnpm dev`". It becomes `` `pnpm dev` `` in markdown and is spoken as its text, like the rest of the sentence.
- **A code block:** `<pre>` or `<pre><code>`. It becomes a fenced block. When it's its own unit, the describer describes it. When it sits inside a list unit, it's silent today.
- **A listing with no code tags:** lines built from styled `<div>`/`<span>` elements, a pattern some highlighters use. Turndown sees only text. The recipe has to wrap it in a `<pre>` for it to become a code block, which `recipes.md` already describes.

Your answers to annotations 5 and 6 go beyond code. They also cover images, so the rule is now about everything that becomes its own unit.

```
System design: Markdown and lists
├─ 1 What a unit's display markdown carries                              open
│  ├─ Vocabulary                                                         settled
│  │  ✓ unit kinds stay paragraph / code / image
│  │  ✓ a paragraph unit's display is GFM
│  │  ✓ headings are paragraph units carrying #, quotes carry >
│  │  ✓ tables are pipe tables, strikethrough is ~~, task lists keep [x] / [ ]
│  │  ✓ a formula is its alttext as plain text, no delimiter
│  │  ✓ attributions, <dl>, footnotes and self-links in headings are left out
│  │  ✓ inline elements with no GFM form keep whatever Turndown outputs for them
│  ├─ List boundaries                                                    open
│  │  ✓ a list is one unit; nested lists stay inside their outer list's unit
│  │  ✓ ordered lists keep their numbers, including start
│  │  ✓ a list splits around every block that becomes its own unit (a code block or an image),
│  │    at any nesting depth, so the describer describes it; the part after continues the numbering
│  │  ✓ inline code stays inside the list item
│  │  ❔ Q2 how a split nested list resumes
│  ├─ Units split around images                                          open
│  │  ✓ an image inside a list item or a table cell is taken out and becomes its own unit
│  │  ❔ Q5 where an image from a table cell goes
│  ├─ The title                                                          settled
│  │  ✓ the title is the first unit, built from extraction.title
│  │  ✓ its display is # <title>
│  │  ✓ no other unit carries the title; the prompt tells the agent to leave out a heading that repeats it
│  └─ Situations                                                         settled
│     ✓ a list or a table inside a blockquote is read the same way as outside one
│     ✓ not considered: a table cell holding a list or a code block
├─ 2 How an element becomes markdown                                     pending
├─ 3 What a recipe must do                                               pending
├─ 4 How the spoken form is derived from the display                     pending
├─ 5 How line structure reaches the audio                                pending
└─ 6 How existing recipes and items get the new behaviour                pending
```

I took "read the same" in annotation 7 to mean a list or table inside a quote needs no special treatment, so the quote stays one unit holding the list or table.

❓ **Q2** - **How a split nested list resumes**: A code block in a nested item splits the list at that depth. What comes before the code closes at a nested level. What comes after starts partway through the inner list, and its parent item was in the earlier unit. GFM has no way to say "continue this inner list under an item from the previous unit". A `start` only continues the numbering of the list it sits on. How the part after the code keeps its nesting, and which numbering it continues (the inner list's, the outer list's, or both), is undecided. The answer determines the rule the prompt gives in branch 3, and how the part after the code is read aloud in branch 4.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Where an image from a table cell goes**: The image comes out of the cell and becomes its own unit. A table is one unit, and each row is spoken as "Header: cell, …". Where the image unit sits relative to the table is undecided, and so is what stays in the cell it came from. The answer affects the table's pipe markdown in `display`, the table's spoken form in branch 4, and the order the listener hears things in.

# Round 4 — findings

## Question A — are sanitize_spoken steps 2-4 still needed?

**Prod-data (describer output, code/image units): zero diffs across all 8 items.** Steps 2-4
on vs off produced byte-identical output for every persisted `spoken` string in
`reports/prod-data/itm_*.json` — describer text is plain English written by an LLM, never
markdown, so it carries none of `**`/`_`/`` ` ``/`~~` to begin with. Steps 2-4 are a pure
no-op there.

**Round-4 units: 4 diffs out of ~50 non-list/code/image units, in `list_mode=items`.**
- `runin-r4` (`**review.**Agents`): ON turns the marker into the word-boundary space that
  makes this "review. Agents"; OFF leaves the literal asterisks glued to the next word.
  Audible, still needed.
- `tbl-3` (`**Design doc first**` table cell): same pattern — ON strips the bold marker
  cleanly; OFF reads the literal asterisks. Audible, still needed.
- `list-9` (checkbox list): ON vs OFF differ only in a doubled space after `[x]`/`[ ]` (a
  GFM-plugin bullet-spacing artifact). Not audible — cosmetic only.
- `math-2` (the display-mode formula): ON *deletes* the literal `*` in
  `value_0 * 2^{-days_since_decision}`, because step 2's marker-strip regex matches any bare
  `*` character regardless of whether markdown-it actually parsed it as emphasis. This `*`
  is round 4's own bare-alttext math substitution (no delimiters, per the settled rule) —
  it's a multiplication sign, not markdown. **Audible and wrong**: the spoken formula loses
  its times-operator entirely.

**Answer: still needed, but not safe as written.** GFM markdown still produces real
`**`/`_`/`` ` ``/`~~` sequences that must be stripped (run-in emphasis, table cells) — turndown
moving off trafilatura didn't remove that need. But sanitize's step 2 is a blind regex over
the joined *text*, not a check on markdown-it's own token classification, so it cannot tell
a markdown marker from a literal character that happens to look like one. Round 4's own math
rule is the first case in this spike to actually put a literal `*` into spoken text, and it
exposes the gap immediately. A safer step 2 would strip based on the parser's own
emphasis/strong token boundaries rather than a raw-text regex; not attempted here since it's
outside this round's settled scope — noted for a future round.

## Question B — what does the TTS do with these cases?

Modal auth and the app lookup (`modal.Cls.from_name('nagara-tts', 'Kokoro')`) worked on the
first try, no blocker. All 11 cases synthesized; see `audio/manifest.json` for exact text and
duration per file, `audio/LISTEN.md` for what to listen for.

**Kokoro's own default (`KPipeline.__call__`'s `split_pattern='\n+'`) already splits on
newlines internally**, and `tts/app.py`'s `_synth_paragraph` concatenates every resulting
chunk with **zero gap** — the `PAUSE_S` silence in `app.py` only sits between separate
entries of the `paragraphs` list argument, never between kokoro's own internal
newline-splits inside one paragraph string. So a round-4 newline-joined list is, in the
final audio, N independently-synthesized fragments glued back-to-back with no pause and no
shared prosody across the join — while the same list space-joined stays one single kokoro
call, since a bare space never matches `split_pattern`. This means the newline-vs-space
choice has no timing/pause consequence in the output; whatever a listener notices has to be
a prosody reset at each line boundary, not silence or spacing.

Durations bear this out: newline- and space-joined pairs land within a few hundred
milliseconds of each other (unordered list: 18.98s vs 18.65s; ordered: 14.80s vs 14.70s) —
the total length is nearly identical either way. Two pairs do show a real gap:
`runin-bold-sanitize-off` (22.73s) is 1.5s longer than `-on` (21.23s), and `checkbox-kept`
(10.78s) is 0.6s longer than `checkbox-stripped` (10.15s) — both consistent with the "off"/
"kept" variants literally containing more spoken material (the leftover `**` markers, the
literal `[x]`/`[ ]` brackets). Whether that extra material renders as garbled noise, as
spoken-aloud punctuation ("asterisk", "bracket x bracket"), or as something else, and whether
the per-line prosody resets in the newline-joined lists sound natural or choppy, is the
human's call — I cannot judge audio by ear. See `audio/LISTEN.md`.

## What round 4 changed vs round 3

The isolated fresh author (given only the base recipe contract, the round-4 rules, and the
article — no inventory/findings) settled a clean recipe on its first validator run. Against
round 3:
- the title is now its **own first unit** (`# <title>`), synthesized outside the recipe —
  the inventory's original h-1 expectation, unmet in rounds 0-3, now holds.
- a heading's self-link is **stripped** (h-2) — rounds 0-3 all kept `[text](#id)`.
- a blockquote's `<footer>/<cite>` attribution is **dropped entirely** (bq-3), not kept as a
  trailing quoted line.
- `<dl>` is **dropped wholesale** (dl-1) — a clean answer vs. rounds 0-3's
  term-runs-into-definition mess.
- `<del>` **round-trips correctly** (p-4): `~~rejection~~` in the display, spoken as the
  plain word via markdown-it's now-enabled `strikethrough` rule — rounds 0-3 arrived at the
  same spoken word by accident (turndown had no del rule at all, pre-GFM).
- task-list checkboxes are kept via the **GFM plugin's native rule**, no recipe-side hack.
- tables are **real GFM markdown** (`| --- |`) for the first time, and the promised
  thead-synthesis for a header-less table actually fires (tbl-1/tbl-2 are now visually
  identical, both real tables).
- `<svg aria-label>` becomes a **real image unit** for the first time (svg-1) — rounds 0-3
  ignored it wholesale.
- a list with an embedded code block **splits cleanly around the code** (list-5/6), each
  fragment its own properly-tagged `<ul>`/`<ol>` clone — no whole-list fallback like round 0.
- list items are digit-prefixed (`1.` not `One.`), newline-joined, no forced trailing period.

## New surprises

- **`code-3` (bare `<pre>`, no `<code>`) is now 3-for-3.** Three independently-authored
  recipes across four rounds have all handed the bare `<pre>` straight to `toMarkdown`
  without synthesizing a `<code>` wrapper first, so turndown never recognizes it as a fenced
  block — display loses its fence markers while the unit's `type` still says `code`. This
  reads like a near-certain gap in how the recipe contract communicates "wrap it yourself,"
  not an authoring fluke.
- **The math-2 `*`-deletion bug** (see Question A) — the first time this spike's sanitize
  step has corrupted actual content rather than just missing a delimiter.
- **`details-1` exposes a fusion bug in the general (non-list) spoken path.** The recipe
  keeps `<details>` as one unit (summary + body, two paragraphs). Round 4's "newline between
  paragraphs inside one unit" rule was implemented only in the list-items walker; the plain
  `to_spoken` path used for every non-list unit inserts *no* separator at all between two
  paragraph blocks sharing a unit, so the two fuse into "...one-sentence versionMove the
  argument..." with zero characters between them — worse than a plain merged-to-space
  reading would have been. Not fixed here (out of this round's settled scope) but worth
  flagging directly: any future round that widens the newline-join rule beyond lists needs
  to also cover this path.

# Rules

A branch about how a value is derived from an input, or how a decision is made: what is read, what is kept, what is dropped, what the result looks like and when there is no result. A rule that only one data flow uses lives inside that flow's sub-branch. A rule that several flows share gets its own branch, and the flows refer to it.

## What it covers

The inputs the rule reads and how it reads them, the transformations it applies or deliberately does not apply, the conditions that produce each outcome, the shape of the result, and the condition under which the result is nothing. Where the rule runs and whether every caller runs the same rule. What a validation failure means for the caller.

It does not cover how the result travels or where it is stored, those are data flows. It does not cover the function or module that implements it, that is program design.

## What it needs to question

- Which inputs are read and how: exact names, what happens with a repeated input, with an empty one, with one that cannot be parsed.
- Whether values are kept verbatim or normalized, and if normalized, how.
- What makes the result nothing, and whether a partial result is allowed or the rule is all or nothing.
- Each exclusion or special case, and whether it is still needed once the other decisions of the design are in place. An exclusion that existed to cover a problem another decision already removes is dropped.
- Whether the result is validated before use, where, and what a failed validation means for the caller.
- Where the rule runs and whether it is one shared rule for every caller or varies by caller.

## Representation

A flowchart of the decision, top to bottom: rectangles for steps, diamonds for conditions with quoted labels, circles for the terminal outcomes. Prose under it for what the diagram does not show: how a field is matched, what verbatim means here, why an outcome is treated as nothing.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Incoming input] --> B["Read the expected fields"]
    B --> C["Keep the first value of each field, drop empty values"]
    C --> D{"Any field left?"}
    D -->|No| N((Nothing))
    D -->|Yes| E["Read the secondary source"]
    E --> F{"Present and usable?"}
    F -->|No| J[Result without the secondary value]
    F -->|Yes| G[Result with the secondary value]
    G --> K{"Matches the schema?"}
    J --> K
    K -->|No| N
    K -->|Yes| O((Result))
```

The prose does not restate every box. It states the matching rules, the meaning of each terminal outcome for the caller, and the guarantee the rule gives, for instance that a malformed input can never break the flow that calls it.

The runtime converts every element a recipe hands it with one shared converter, and recipes never convert HTML to markdown themselves. The converter serializes the element including its own tag, so a heading, quote or list keeps what makes it one. It runs Turndown with a fixed configuration: ATX headings, fenced code, `-` bullets, `---` rules. The GFM plugin is added, so tables, strikethrough and task lists are converted too. - Turndown escapes text that looks like markdown, such as a heading starting with `1.`, which came out as `1\.` in production.

Round 5 is done. The conversion can split a list by itself: all 8 cases came out right, including nesting at 2 and 3 levels, two blocks in one list, a list with `start=5`, and text before and after a block in the same item. It also showed that splitting inside the runtime would break how the validator ties units to elements.

**The empty item.** In the raw markdown, the resumed part shows the parent's number and the first nested item on one line: `2.  3.  Item B.3`. It looks collapsed, but it's valid CommonMark. markdown-it parses it as an empty `<li>` holding the resumed nested list, and the spike checked that for all three cases where this shape appears. A renderer that doesn't follow CommonMark could show it differently.

**Where the split would break the validator.** I have these from the round 5 report and haven't re-read the code myself:

# Recipe audit — 2026-09-27

## Task 3 — what happens when a stored recipe fails validation

**Verified.** The workflow neither authors from scratch nor fails the job outright: it hands the
failure to the revision agent, bounded by retries, and the old version stands until a revision
actually settles.

`pipeline/src/workflow/extraction.ts:104-124` — when the job carries a recipe (`recipe != null`),
`guardedRun` runs it first. On `"invalid"` it calls `settleRecipe` with `kind: "revision"`,
`retries: this.env.revisionRetries`, seeded with the failing report and this `exhausted` message:
`"revision gave up: the recipe still fails the article and the old version stands"` (line 121).

`settleRecipe` (`extraction.ts:49-96`) loops up to `1 + retries` attempts, dispatching the revisor
agent (`pipeline/src/agents/revisor.ts`) each time and re-running its settled script through
`guardedRun`. A settlement that runs clean returns `{ state: "complete", ..., recipe: settlement.source }`
(line 85-90); exhausting retries returns `{ state: "error", error: options.exhausted }` — the job
fails and the old version is left in place, never touched.

On the API side, `api/app/service/pipeline/steps.py:177-183` (`ExtractionResolveStep`) checks
`status.recipe is not None` on a `complete` outcome and, when present, calls `insert_recipe_version`:
the comment reads "the job authored or revised the domain's recipe: a pure insert as the next
version, and the item's pointer moves to it." `api/app/service/recipes.py:40-60` confirms the insert
is `version = max + 1`, always a new row — "a revision never updates a row, so nothing is lost by
starting over." So **yes**, a successful revision is stored as a new `recipe_versions` row, and the
item's `recipe_version_id` moves to it; a revision that never settles leaves the prior version as
the domain's latest and fails only the one item.

No domain in production has ever reached a second version (see the table below), so this path is
verified from code, not yet observed in data.

# Markdown and lists: settled design

## 1 What a unit's display markdown carries
- Unit kinds stay paragraph / code / image; a paragraph unit's display is GFM.
- Headings are paragraph units carrying `#`, quotes carry `>`; a list or table inside a quote stays in the quote's unit.
- Tables are GFM pipe tables; strikethrough is `~~`; task lists keep `[x]` / `[ ]`.
- A formula is its alttext as plain text, no delimiter.
- Attributions (blockquote footer/cite), `<dl>`, footnotes (refs and list) and self-links in headings are left out of the units.
- Inline elements with no GFM form keep whatever Turndown outputs.
- A list is one unit; nested lists stay inside their outer list's unit; ordered lists keep their numbers, including `start`.
- A list splits around every code block (`<pre>` / `<pre><code>`) or image inside it, at any depth, so the describer describes it; the part after continues the numbering and opens with an empty item at each enclosing level (compact CommonMark form `2.  3.  Item`), so resumed items keep their depth. Inline code stays inside the item.
- The title is the first unit, `# <title>`, built from extraction.title; no other unit carries the title.
- Not considered: image in a table cell, a table cell holding a list or code.

## 2 How an element becomes markdown
- One shared converter for every recipe; a recipe never converts by hand.
- toMarkdown serializes the element including its own tag (today it uses cheerio `.html()`, the inner HTML, which drops the tag: the cause of 0/53 headings with `#`, 0/16 quotes with `>`, ordered lists as `-` in production).
- A `<pre>` without a `<code>` child gets its content wrapped in `<code>` before conversion, so every `<pre>` becomes a fenced block.
- Turndown with the fixed config (ATX, fenced, `-`, `---`) plus the GFM plugin.
- The validator checks the units the recipe declared (real element paths, checks unchanged). After a clean validation, the runtime splits list units holding a code block or an image into list part / code or image unit / list part, converts each part with the same converter, prepends the title unit, and returns the flattened list: what crosses to the API and what the agent's extract tool shows.
- Not considered: telling code `<pre>` from non-code, empty markdown for a declared element, a table with no header row, Turndown's escaping.

## 3 What a recipe must do
- Prompt: markdown is GFM, hand toMarkdown the whole element; a list is one unit, never one per `<li>`, even with code or images; the runtime may split a unit into several and the extract tool shows the split result; formulas as plain alttext, no delimiter; leave out attributions, `<dl>`, footnotes, heading self-links and any heading repeating the title, through the recipe's own includes/ignores (leftover check unchanged); keep task-list checkboxes.
- The author and revision prompts carry the same rules.
- Validator: an `<li>` without a wrapping `<ol>`/`<ul>` is a problem, sent back for revision; no other prompt rule is checked; no check that headings/quotes/lists kept their markdown.
- Not considered: an agent failing a rule after its revisions run out.

## 4 How the spoken form is derived from the display
- Derived from display by walking its markdown token tree.
- Headings, quotes and the title unit are read as their words, markers dropped.
- Every block inside a unit is on its own line (newline); nothing runs together (today paragraphs and list items fuse: `'First itemSecond item'`).
- A list item is its own line, no full stop added; ordered items keep `1.` at the start of the line; nesting depth is not announced.
- A split list's empty item has no spoken line.
- Task checkboxes are stripped; struck-through text is read as its words with no sign.
- A table's header row is spoken on its own line, then each body row as "Header: cell, …" on its own line.
- Code and image units keep their current spoken forms and the describer.
- Sanitize tail: keeps stripping leftover emphasis/code markers (still needed for run-in emphasis from Turndown); an asterisk only when it touches text; keeps newlines; only a `<word>` pair reduces to its word; then operator sequences become words, longest match first: `<=` less than or equal to, `>=` greater than or equal to, `->` to, `=>` to, `<-` from, `<<` much less than, `>>` much greater than, `<3` heart, `<` less than, `>` greater than. The describer's output runs through the same tail.
- Not considered: formula LaTeX read character by character, a line inside a unit with nothing to pronounce.

## 5 How line structure reaches the audio
- One spoken string per unit, lines separated by newlines; the synthesizer's input shape is unchanged; tts/ does not change.
- Kokoro splits at newlines by default and the service joins the line audio with no gap; the newline is not named in the TTS contract.
- The inter-unit pause and one timing window per unit are unchanged.
- Not considered: very long lists split into Kokoro's own chunks, consecutive blank lines.

## 6 How existing recipes and items get the new behaviour
- Runtime changes reach every stored recipe on its next run.
- The four recipes that break the new rules (blog.dyanacek.com, newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com, harper.blog, ngrislain.github.io; see reports/recipe-audit.md) are edited by hand during implementation, overwriting their stored version row, going live with the runtime change.
- A stored recipe that fails the validator on a later run goes to the revision agent with bounded retries (existing behaviour).
- Not considered: regenerating already-extracted items, jobs running during the deploy, release order of pipeline and API.

## Documentation plan
- New note: `docs/technical-design/markdown-units.md` for branches 1 and 2.
- Existing notes to update: recipes.md, extraction-service.md, article-extraction.md, item-contract.md, the-describer.md, tts-service.md, product-design/what-gets-read-aloud.md (pending the stale-info scout).

# Write documentation

A note explains how a part works, in the present tense, and it is what someone reads instead of the code when they need to understand that part. This skill writes one, or brings one back in line with the code.

Resolve the docs folder as `docs` says, and read the charter and the target folder's README before writing a line. The charter decides the headings, the callouts, the diagrams, the wrapping, the frontmatter, the naming rule and how the indexes work. Where it is more specific than anything here, it wins. This skill carries no template body.

Most of the time a draft already exists. When mahou:design hands over a tree, each settled branch carries mechanism-first prose and a validated diagram, and writing the note is mostly moving that text into place. When the user asks for a mechanism to be written up, the code is the source and a `mahou:code-scout` reads it so the reading stays out of this conversation.

## 1. Pick the folder, and say which

Use the charter's folder table and, when the project's `CLAUDE.md` has a section on where each kind of change is documented, that section. Announce the folder and the reason in one line before writing. A note in the wrong folder is worse than a missing one, because readers find it, trust it and never look for a second copy.

Search the folder first and **prefer extending the note that already covers it**. A new section in the right note beats a new note beside it, and near-duplicates are how an index stops being readable. Check the name against every file in the docs folder before creating one; the charter usually says why a collision matters.

## 2. Write it

The charter owns the shape. The content rules are the framework's:

**Overview, then mechanism.** The overview says what the part is and is responsible for, in a few sentences a reader can stop after. Then the shape of the data, what calls what, in what order, in the sections from the template's menu that the subject needs and in the order that reads best, as `docs` describes. This is the bulk of it. A reader should be able to follow the part without opening the source.

**Explain the code, do not reprint it.** A declaration belongs in the file it lives in, where it is typechecked and stays current. What a reader cannot get from that file is why each part exists and who asks it, so the surface goes in a table of what each member answers, and the behaviour goes in prose or a diagram. A snippet survives only where the code *is* the insight, at two to four lines.

**The reasoning goes beside the thing it justifies, never as the note's structure.** Opening with the argument makes the reader meet the case for the design before the design. Keep the argument, since it is what lets a decision be revisited rather than re-argued, in the callout form the charter names, next to the mechanism. State the actual reason, not its provenance: "a strict test would freeze a thing already overlapping a wall", not "because the investigation showed".

**Every section explains something that exists.** A section that only introduces, summarizes or lists what other sections hold does not belong.

**A diagram whenever the subject has a shape.** A state machine, a data model, a sequence or a request's path all read faster drawn. Follow the charter's convention; where it names mermaid, do not draw in ASCII, and validate every diagram with superpowers:mermaid-validation before the draft is shown.

**Strip the working session out of the note.** The tree or code a note comes from may name projects, tools, repositories and the current implementation; the note gets shared, so the draft drops them. In the draft:

- Name roles, not products, when the design is generic: "the assistant" rather than a product's name, unless the design is that product's alone.
- Name another note or tool only when the design depends on it, and then as a link at the point of dependency.
- No component, library or package names.
- No description of the current implementation or of what a repository still lacks; those descriptions belong to tasks.
- No sentences about who owns a piece of work.
- Never describe the prototype's controls or its file.
- Cut any sentence that compares the design with how things work today.

## 3. Describe the present

No "used to", no "previously", no "no longer", no "replaced by". A rejected alternative is *considered and not chosen, because…*, a standing reason, not a history of the argument.

This matters most when updating, which is most of the time. Change only what actually changed; if a section still describes the code correctly, leave it exactly as it is. Insert new behaviour without disturbing what is there. Delete behaviour that is gone; do not annotate it as removed. A note rewritten wholesale to accommodate one paragraph is a diff nobody can check.

## 4. Check the draft before anyone sees it

Run superpowers:unslop over the draft. It governs the prose; where it disagrees with the charter or the template about form, the charter wins. The known case is emoji heading prefixes, which unslop removes and the seeded template requires; the same holds for callout syntax and for bold on domain terms the charter asks for. Then dispatch a `mahou:documentation-reviewer` with the draft, the charter, the folder README and the template, and apply what it reports: those are departures from rules the project wrote for itself, so applying them is not a decision. Anything it reports that turns on the content rather than the form goes to the user as a question.

Then show the whole draft in the conversation and wait. Nothing lands in a file the user has not seen.

## 5. Land it in its index

Write the agreed draft. **Link it from at least one existing note**, or nobody reads it.

Then check how the folder's index works. A generated index means the note appears by existing, *provided its tag is right*: confirm the tag against the charter and the neighbouring notes, because a wrong tag drops a note out of its index silently, with no error anywhere. A hand-maintained table means adding this note's row and nothing else; do not touch the others.

## 6. Say what you wrote

Which note, which folder, which sections are new or changed, and what you deliberately left untouched. If reasoning went into a callout, quote it: it is the part written on the user's behalf, and it is short enough to read.

title: "nagara: docs"
summary: "The docs: what each folder holds, how files are named, and how to write a note."

# nagara: docs

## What each folder holds

| Folder | Holds | Index |
|---|---|---|
| `technical-design/` | How the code works: the item lifecycle, article extraction, read-along timing, the TTS service, the item contract, persistence and storage, authentication, deployment and CI, the invariants | [Technical design](technical-design/README.md) |
| `product-design/` | What nagara is: the ながら聞き premise, the listening experience, what gets read aloud, the queue | [Product design](product-design/README.md) |

Which folder a note belongs in is a question about its subject, not about who wrote it. Code reading as a short placeholder rather than being read aloud is product design: it is a statement about what a listener experiences. The markdown-it-py token walk that produces that placeholder is technical design. The 100 ms inter-paragraph pause is product design, a number about how listening feels; folding it into the preceding timing window so there is no dead highlight zone is technical design. A note that needs both goes wherever it is mostly about and links across.

`_templates/` holds no notes. The underscore is a sorting convention and nothing more: it floats the folder to the top of the file explorer.

Work in flight lives in Linear, not here. A note describes something that exists; the issue that asked for it, and the open questions around it, live on the nagara project there. A note never links to an issue: the issue closes and the link rots, while the note is maintained for as long as the part exists.

## Naming

A note is named after the aspect it explains, in kebab-case. Not after its folder, not numbered, not dated: a date is a frontmatter field, so an index can sort on it without every filename carrying one.

File names are unique across the whole docs folder, so a link never has to be disambiguated. Before adding a note, check the name is not taken.

Every folder's index is called `README.md`, so that name is the one deliberate collision here: the payoff is that each index renders as a folder front page when the repository is browsed on the web. A link to a folder's index names the folder: `[the technical design](technical-design/README.md)`.

## Frontmatter

Every note carries `title` and `summary`, plus `created`. The summary is what shows up in search, in hover previews and in the indexes, so write it as a sentence about the subject rather than about the note.

## How to write a note

**A note explains how one part works.** It opens with an overview a reader can stop after, then the mechanism: the shape of the data, what calls what, in what order, with a diagram when the subject is a flow, a tree or a sequence. A reader should be able to hold that part of the system in their head without opening `api/app` or `tts/app.py` first.

`_templates/note.md` offers the sections a note can use. They are a menu, not a required shape and not a closed list: keep the ones the subject needs, add one the menu lacks when the subject asks for it, and order them so the note is easiest to follow rather than in the order the template lists them. Edge cases and failure modes go in the prose or in a callout, never in a section of their own.

**Reasoning goes in a callout, beside the thing it justifies**, not as the spine of the note:

```markdown
> [!NOTE] Why no headless browser
> A plain fetch handled every HTML fixture tried, including a JS-rendered Substack post: it server-renders its content. The boundary sits further out than assumed.
```

A note that opens with the argument for a design makes the reader meet the case for the architecture before the architecture itself, and the argument is not what they came for. It is still worth keeping (it is what lets a decision be revisited rather than re-argued); it just is not the spine. Per-decision *why* is also the one thing the code already has, densely, at the point of each decision; what code cannot give anyone is the shape of the whole.

Three callout kinds, and they mean different things:

- `> [!NOTE]`: a real choice, and why it went that way.
- `> [!WARNING]`: a failure mode: what breaks, how it presents, and whether anything catches it. Prefer failures that have actually happened.
- `> [!TIP]`: an alternative considered and not taken, with the reason it was not.

**A note is not a decision record.** There is no requirements table, no acceptance criteria, no user story, no status ladder. Those describe work being planned; a note describes something that exists.

**A note describes the present.** No "used to", no "previously", no "no longer". An alternative that was rejected is *considered and not chosen, because…*, a standing reason, not a history of the argument.

Create a note from `_templates/note.md`. Then **link it from at least one existing note** and add its row to its folder's index: a note nothing links to does not get read.

## House style

- **No hard wrapping.** One line per paragraph; let the editor wrap. Diffs then show changed sentences rather than reflowed blocks.
- **Explain the code, do not reprint it.** A note is not a second copy of a declaration. What each member answers goes in a table, behaviour goes in a diagram or in prose, and a snippet appears only where the code itself is the insight: an exact formula, a guard whose precise form is the point. Two to four lines when it happens. Written the other way, a note comes out a third fenced code, in a second place where nothing typechecks it and it quietly falls out of date.
- **Mermaid, not ASCII**, for anything with a shape. A state machine, a data model, a request's path through the system and a tree all read faster as a diagram than as a paragraph describing one, and both GitHub and Obsidian render mermaid.
- **Headings name their subject, and carry an emoji.** "Extraction" and "The extraction" give a reader nothing to search for; "how a URL becomes paragraphs" does. Prefer a heading that could answer a question someone typed into search. Every heading in a note opens with one emoji chosen for its subject (`## 💽 Modeling`, `### 🔑 Login`), so a reader scanning the outline sees the shape of the note before the words; the template carries the usual ones and a section you add picks its own.
- **Say what a thing is.** Staging a sentence against its own opposite ("it does not reject the unknown kind, it ignores it") reads as emphasis while carrying no information the plain form lacks. Write the plain form.
- **Prefer commas, colons and full stops to dashes.** A paragraph leaning on dashes is usually one that wants to be two sentences.
- **Write about our implementation.** A comparison with some other tool belongs inside a callout that justifies a decision, and nowhere else; a note is not a literature review.
- Close a note with a `---` rule and a `Related:` line linking the notes it actually touches.

## Adding a folder

A folder is three things, and they have to agree:

1. The directory.
2. A `README.md` in it, carrying that folder's index.
3. A row in the folder table above.

`mahou:init` will do all three and leave anything that already exists alone, or do it by hand from this list: the skills read what is here either way. What breaks is doing two of the three: a folder with no row is invisible to anyone reading this file, and a row with no folder sends people looking for something that is not there.

# Program architecture

Takes a design the user has settled and works out the architecture of the program that implements it: how the code is distributed and shipped, what the program does from its entrypoint to its exit, and what each part agrees with the rest.

## What the level is

`design` stops above endpoints, functions and files. This skill starts there and stops short of the code.

The decisions it settles are the ones a reader meets before they read a function body. Package names, command and flag names, configuration keys, the names and members of the contracts between parts, the order of calls, what a failure at each step does: those are examples of the level, not a list of it. Whatever else has to be decided before the program can be written belongs here too.

The decisions it leaves alone are the ones the code itself carries. Function signatures, the module-by-module file list inside a part and test cases are examples again, and so is anything else a reader could paste.

A leaf that could be answered differently, and would change what a reader of the finished program sees, belongs here. A leaf the design, the language or a library already answers is not a leaf.

The proof of the program, its test cases and manual validations, is not designed here either. mahou:test-design derives it from the settled design once this tree is complete.

## Opening

1. Read the settled design, or the notes that record it. A `mahou:docs-scout` reads the notes so they stay out of this conversation.

2. List what has to be designed, ordered so each item builds on the last:

   - How the code is distributed: packages, what is published, what is built and how it runs.
   - What the program does: the entrypoint, the order of the steps, what each failure does, what the process returns.
   - One item per part the flow named, for its contract.

3. Wait for the user's corrections. Drop items that are code, absorb items that belong inside another, and add the ones the design requires.

4. Build the tree. The root is "Program architecture" and each item is a branch, every branch pending.

## Working a branch

As `design` describes it, against its types table extended with the rows below. When a branch matches one of `design`'s own types, use that reference as written.

| The branch is about | Reference |
|---|---|
| How the code is distributed, published and run | `references/types/package-layout.md` |
| What the program does in order, and what it returns | `references/types/control-flow.md` |

A branch that fits no row in either table is worked out with the user, as in `design`.

## Recording

As `design` describes it, except that the notes describe parts of a program. A part with no note gets one. When a note already describes the same part at the design's level, extend it rather than write a second one, since two notes about one part end up contradicting each other.

## What this skill is not

It does not write code, does not choose function or file names, does not plan the work into issues, and does not commit.

## What it needs to question

- How many packages, and what belongs in each. A package exists because something outside it depends on it separately.
- Which packages are published, under which names, and whether a folder's name is the name published to the registry.
- Whether there is a build step. What it produces, what it costs to keep, and what a consumer gets without one.
- What a user invokes, and what executes it. When the answer is a compiled form, what that form takes away: a plug-in loaded at run time, a dependency resolved from disk, a patch applied by a package manager.
- Where tests sit relative to the code they test.
- The minimum runtime version, and which decision above forces it.
- A dependency that must be changed to work: whether it is patched, forked into a package or replaced, and whether that fix reaches an installed copy.

## Representation

A file tree in a fenced block, annotated, then a paragraph per package saying what it is for and what depends on it. A file tree is the one shape this type does not draw in mermaid. The annotations beside each entry are half the content, and mermaid has no form that can show them.

```
<repository>/
├── package.json                 what the whole workspace runs
├── <workspace file>
└── packages/
    ├── <tool>/
    │   ├── package.json         what a user invokes
    │   ├── src/
    │   └── tests/
    └── <shared>/
        ├── package.json
        ├── src/                 what more than one package needs
        └── tests/
```

The prose does not restate the tree. It says why each package is separate, what it exposes to the others, and which decisions above the tree cannot show: what is published, what is built, what runs it.
